# Poker hand rankings

*All ten poker hands from best to worst, how often each one shows up, and how ties are broken.*

3 min read · Updated 2026-09-26

Every poker game in this guide uses the same ten hands. A hand is always **exactly five cards** — in Hold'em you pick the best five from your two cards plus the five on the board. The rarer a hand is, the higher it ranks.

## Best to worst

> **1. Royal flush:** `A♠ K♠ Q♠ J♠ 10♠`
>
> A-K-Q-J-10, all one suit.

> **2. Straight flush:** `9♥ 8♥ 7♥ 6♥ 5♥`
>
> Five in a row, all one suit.

> **3. Four of a kind:** `Q♣ Q♦ Q♥ Q♠ 7♦`
>
> Four cards of one rank.

> **4. Full house:** `K♥ K♦ K♠ 4♣ 4♥`
>
> Three of a kind plus a pair. Say it “kings full of fours”.

> **5. Flush:** `A♦ J♦ 8♦ 6♦ 2♦`
>
> Any five of one suit.

> **6. Straight:** `10♣ 9♦ 8♠ 7♥ 6♣`
>
> Five in a row, mixed suits.

> **7. Three of a kind:** `7♣ 7♦ 7♠ K♥ 2♣`
>
> Three cards of one rank.

> **8. Two pair:** `J♥ J♣ 5♦ 5♠ A♥`
>
> Two different pairs.

> **9. One pair:** `10♠ 10♣ A♥ 8♦ 4♠`
>
> Two cards of one rank.

> **10. High card:** `A♣ Q♦ 9♥ 6♠ 3♣`
>
> Nothing else — “ace high”.

## How often you get each hand

The first column is the chance of being dealt the hand in five cards — the numbers the ranking is built on. The second is the chance a Hold'em player’s best five out of seven cards (two hole cards plus a full board) is that hand.

**Straight flush excludes royal flushes; flush and straight exclude straight flushes.**

| Hand | Dealt 5 cards | Best of 7 cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Royal flush | 1 in 649,740 | 1 in 30,940 (0.003%) |
| Straight flush | 1 in 72,193 | 1 in 3,591 (0.03%) |
| Four of a kind | 1 in 4,165 | 1 in 595 (0.17%) |
| Full house | 1 in 694 | 2.6% |
| Flush | 1 in 509 | 3.0% |
| Straight | 1 in 255 | 4.6% |
| Three of a kind | 1 in 47 | 4.8% |
| Two pair | 1 in 21 | 23.5% |
| One pair | 42.3% | 43.8% |
| High card | 50.1% | 17.4% |

> **Note — Why doesn’t the order change in Hold'em?:** With seven cards, three of a kind is only a little more common than a straight, and high card is rarer than one pair. The ranking still follows the five-card odds — that’s the rule everywhere, so don’t let anyone argue otherwise.

## Breaking ties

- **Suits never count.** Two flushes of the same ranks split the pot.
- **Compare the part that makes the hand first**, then the leftover cards (the **kickers**) from highest to lowest.
- **Two pair:** higher pair first, then the lower pair, then the kicker.
- **Full house:** the three of a kind decides first. Kings full of twos beats queens full of aces.
- **Flush and high card:** compare the highest card, then the next, down to the fifth.
- **Straights:** the top card decides. The ace can be low in A-2-3-4-5 (the lowest straight), but a straight can’t wrap around: Q-K-A-2-3 is not a straight.

> **You:** `K♠ Q♣` · Board: `K♦ 9♣ 7♠ 4♥ 2♦`
>
> Pair of kings with a queen kicker.

> **Opponent:** `K♥ J♦` · Board: `K♦ 9♣ 7♠ 4♥ 2♦`
>
> Also a pair of kings, but the jack kicker loses to your queen.

> **The board plays:** `8♣ 8♦` · Board: `A♠ K♠ Q♦ J♣ 10♥`
>
> The board is already a straight to the ace that nobody can beat. Everyone still in the hand splits the pot — even with a pair of eights.

## Quick memory trick

Flush beats straight, full house beats flush. If you forget, remember that it’s easier to collect five cards in a row than five of one suit — and easier still to get three of a kind.
